> The alternative was a field in the outer's metadata, but the outer's leaf is inserted before its inner transactions run and OpenView::rawTxInsert does not replace a leaf.

Interesting 

Yeah, conceptually if the outer transaction's only effect is to add/queue the inners, then backtracking and updating the metadata is a little murky and sets a precedent. 

On the other hand, you have a result attached to the the known outer txn id, which is more easy to consume than having to retrieve and parse the whole ledger's transactions which is the naive consequence barring updating rpc handlers to do the scan, potentially using indexes. 

Using metadata would probably also save some bytes, reusing existing txn/serialization instead of a new key/leaf. 

Murky 🤔 

Then again, maybe transactions are just the atoms, and batches, as long as they are comprised of contiguous atoms, can be thought of some bigger unit: transactions / batches / ledgers.

prs.body:
## High Level Overview of Change

Adds the `BatchV2` amendment and a `ttBATCH_RESULT` (`BatchResult`) pseudo-transaction. When a `Batch` applies with `tesSUCCESS` in a closed ledger, `applyTransaction` inserts a `BatchResult` right after the batch's inner transactions. It carries the outer's ID in `sfParentBatchID` and lists every inner transaction the batch attempted, in order, as `sfTransactionHash` and `sfEngineResultCode`.

## Context of Change

An inner transaction that fails with a `tem`, `tef` or `ter` code leaves nothing in the ledger, and neither does any inner transaction of a rolled-back `tfAllOrNothing` batch. The outer's metadata covers only its own fee and sequence, so the only record of what a batch did is the `BatchTrace` log line on the node that applied it. #8164 keeps those results in a node-local table; this puts them in the ledger, so every node, Clio and explorer reads the same answer.

The record cannot be agreed in the transaction set like `ttFEE` or `ttAMENDMENT`, because its content exists only after execution. It is generated during the ledger build, as the inner transactions already are, from the outer ID and the inner IDs and results only, so every node produces the same leaf. It is inserted into the view the outer applied to, after the batch view is committed or dropped, so a rollback cannot remove it. The alternative was a field in the outer's metadata, but the outer's leaf is inserted before its inner transactions run and `OpenView::rawTxInsert` does not replace a leaf.

An entry was applied when its result is `tes` or `tec` and the batch was not rolled back; an inner transaction missing from `sfBatchResults` was never attempted. `sfEngineResultCode` is `INT32` because `tem`, `tef` and `ter` codes are negative.

`isPseudoTx` covers the new type, so it cannot be submitted or relayed, and `Change` preflight rejects it with `temINVALID` on any view, including from a proposed transaction set. Ledger replay skips it, and replaying the outer regenerates it.

## API Impact

- [x] Public API: New feature (new methods and/or new fields)
- [x] `libxrpl` change (any change that may affect `libxrpl` or dependents of `libxrpl`)

`tx`, `ledger` and the transaction streams return the new `BatchResult` transaction type once `BatchV2` is enabled.

## Future Tasks

- Amend XLS-0056 to specify `BatchResult`.

> How does this handle transactions that occur during downtime?

Could these outcomes live in the outer Batch’s metadata, perhaps as an array aligned with `RawTransactions`, with a defined encoding for negative engine results and applied/skipped status?

prs.body:
## High Level Overview of Change

A validated `Batch` can have inner transactions that did nothing. An inner transaction that fails with a `ter`, `tem` or `tef` code is never applied, so it has no metadata and is not in the ledger at all. Under `tfAllOrNothing` the rollback also discards the inner transaction that had succeeded. The only record of either case today is the `BatchTrace` debug log line in `apply.cpp`, which is a log line, not something a client can query.

This PR records each inner transaction's outcome while the node builds a validated ledger and returns it from `tx`:

```json
"inner_results": [
  { "hash": "F137AEA3…", "result": "tesSUCCESS", "applied": false },
  { "hash": "A056A319…", "result": "terPRE_SEQ", "applied": false }
]
```

The array is in `RawTransactions` order. `applied` is whether the inner transaction's changes ended up in the ledger, so `tesSUCCESS` with `applied: false` is the rolled-back case.

### Context of Change

`applyBatchTransactions` gets an optional collector and pushes a `BatchInnerResult` (`parentBatchId`, `innerTxId`, `index`, `ter`, `applied`) per inner transaction it runs. When a `tfAllOrNothing` batch rolls back it marks everything it recorded as not applied. Only `BuildLedger` (consensus build and replay) passes a collector; the open ledger never does, so trial applies are not recorded. The results ride on the built `Ledger` as side data that is not part of the hash, and `saveValidatedLedger` writes them to a new `BatchInnerResults` table in `transaction.db`, in the same SQLite transaction as `Transactions` and `AccountTransactions`. The table is gated by `use_tx_tables` and pruned with the other tx tables by `online_delete`.

Recording at validated-ledger save rather than on the apply path is deliberate. An earlier version of this wrote rows from inside `applyBatchTransactions` on every pass, so an open-ledger trial apply and the consensus apply of the same inner transaction overwrote each other, and every inner transaction cost a synchronous SQLite commit in the apply path. Here the apply path only appends to a vector.

One limitation: a node that acquired a ledger from the network instead of building it has no rows for that ledger, and `tx` omits the field. Rows are keyed by `LedgerSeq`, so the gap is visible rather than silently wrong.

### API Impact

- [x] Public API: New feature (new methods and/or new fields)
- [ ] Public API: Breaking change (in general, breaking changes should only impact the next api_version)
- [x] `libxrpl` change (any change that may affect `libxrpl` or dependents of `libxrpl`)
- [ ] Peer protocol change (must be backward compatible or bump the peer protocol version)

`tx` gains `inner_results` (API-CHANGELOG updated in this PR). In `libxrpl`, `applyTransaction` takes an optional trailing `std::vector<BatchInnerResult>*`, and `Ledger` gains `setBatchInnerResults` / `batchInnerResults`. Existing callers are unchanged.

## Test Plan

`Batch_test` gains `inner results`: a `tfAllOrNothing` batch with a future-sequence inner returns two entries, `tesSUCCESS` and `terPRE_SEQ`, both `applied: false`, and the rolled-back inner is `txnNotFound`; a `tfIndependent` batch returns both `applied: true` in order; inner transactions and non-Batch transactions have no field. The full `Batch` suite and the ledger, tx and rpc suites pass; levelization results are unchanged.

## High Level Overview of Change

A top-level JSON array is the batch form the specification defines, accepted from API version 3. Each entry is a request in its own right, nesting its parameters as a lone request does and correlating by its own `id`. The answer is an array of one reply per entry at HTTP 200, as the `method: "batch"` form answers. All entries of one body must name the same `api_version`, or name none and inherit the body's, and a body whose entries disagree is refused whole. One body then has one version, which is what makes a 100-entry cap answerable: a cap that read a version off one entry could be side-stepped by reordering the entries, or by naming the version where the cap did not look, so the cap reads the body's one version, found wherever dispatch would find it.

## Context of Change

Refusing a mixed body is a break a version 1 or 2 client can see, recorded as such in `API-CHANGELOG.md`. A `method: "batch"` body whose entries name different versions is served today, each entry at its own version, and is refused from now on; one whose entries agree keeps working, and below version 3 that form stays uncapped.

Five conditions reject a whole array: empty, over the cap, holding nothing that could be a request, naming a version below 3 or one the server cannot serve, and naming two different versions across its entries. Four answer one specification error object with a null `id`, an array naming none; an array holding nothing that could be a request answers one such object per entry, as the specification shows. Each reaches every API version, since no earlier version accepts an array.

## API Impact

- [x] Public API: New feature (new methods and/or new fields)
- [x] Public API: Breaking change (in general, breaking changes should only impact the next api_version)

## High Level Overview of Change

Allows Single Asset Vault and Lending Protocol transactions to run as Batch inner transactions
when `featureLendingProtocolV1_2` is enabled. Before the amendment, these transaction types remain
invalid inside a Batch.

## Context of Change

Batch already applies inner transactions through the normal transaction pipeline, but explicitly
rejects all Vault and Lending transaction types.

This change gates that restriction on `featureLendingProtocolV1_2`. It also verifies the special
authorization flow for `LoanSet`, where both parties sign the outer Batch instead of using an
inner `CounterpartySignature`.

## API Impact

- [x] `libxrpl` change (any change that may affect `libxrpl` or dependents of `libxrpl`)

## Test Plan

`Batch_test`:

- rejection of Vault and Lending inner transactions before the amendment;
- successful Vault creation and deposit after the amendment;
- required `LoanSet` counterparty and Batch signer validation;
- successful `LoanSet` and cover deposit in one Batch;
- rollback of a `LoanSet` when a later inner transaction fails.

New `LendingBatch` suite, each case run with `LendingProtocolV1_1` on and off:

- vault lifecycle in one Batch: `VaultCreate`, `VaultDeposit`, `VaultWithdraw`, `VaultDelete`,
  on an open-ended vault and on a closed-ended vault in the Subscription phase;
- loan lifecycle: `VaultCreate`, `VaultDeposit`, `LoanBrokerSet`, `LoanSet`, `LoanPay`. One Batch
  on an open-ended vault with V1_1 off. Two Batches on a closed-ended vault with V1_1 on, split
  at the Subscription to Investment boundary, because `VaultDeposit` and `LoanSet` are only
  valid in different phases;
- arbitrage under `tfAllOrNothing`: `LoanSet`, DEX buy, DEX sell, `LoanPay`. One run that
  profits and one where the sell offer cannot fill and nothing persists;
- `LoanManage` default and `LoanBrokerCoverWithdraw` in one Batch, once the grace period of a
  loan created earlier has passed;
- `tfIndependent` chains where a failing inner (`VaultWithdraw`, `VaultDelete`, `LoanPay`) does
  not stop the inners after it.

Part 15/28 of a stack. Base: part 14 (`bthomee/shamap-invalid-11-revive-timer`).

## High Level Overview of Change

`TransactionAcquire::takeNodes()` now accumulates one combined verdict across a whole batch instead of
stopping at the first bad node, so a packet that ends badly still gets credit (and clears the
timeout-postponing progress flag) for the good nodes ahead of it, matching what
`InboundLedger::receiveNode()` already does.

### Context of Change

`TransactionAcquire::takeNodes()` accumulates one `SHAMapAddNode` across the batch and hands it back, so
a packet ending on one bad node still counts the nodes hooked in ahead of it. A root the set already
holds counts as a duplicate rather than passing unremarked, which is what tells a batch of nodes we
already have from one that was never examined at all.

The body moves to `takeNodesLocked()` and `takeNodes()` becomes a thin wrapper that takes the lock and
records what the batch achieved on the one exit, since several of the inner exits stop the batch
early and
nothing in the compiler catches one that forgets to record progress. Progress turns on the batch being
useful rather than good, so a batch of nothing but duplicates records none: that flag is what keeps the
next timer tick from counting a timeout, and a reply carrying nothing new advanced nothing. It costs
retry budget on the ordinary second responder to a fan-out and nothing else.

`InboundTransactions::gotData()` asks `isGood()` rather than `isUseful()` for the useless-data charge,
which keeps that duplicate free. Now that the verdict distinguishes a duplicate from an empty tally,
the useful test would charge for it while the batch that was never examined still needs charging.

`testPartialBatchIsCounted` feeds two good nodes followed by one at a position it cannot occupy, and
checks the verdict names both halves and that the flag is set; then a batch of nothing but a root
already held, checking it is good, not useful, and records nothing; then that root alongside a node the
set does need, checking the duplicate is reported as one while the other records the progress.

### API Impact

None of the checkboxes below apply: this is an internal `xrpld` correctness fix with no `libxrpl`,
public-API, or peer-protocol surface.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: A duplicate does not advance the acquisition, so including `getDuplicate() > 0` leaves `progress_` set for a packet containing only nodes already held. A peer can replay that root on every timer interval and prevent `TimeoutCounter` from counting timeouts, potentially keeping the acquisition alive indefinitely; progress should depend only on `san.isUseful()`, with the duplicate-only test adjusted to expect no progress.

reviewCommentsList.author: bthomee
reviewCommentsList.body:
Confirmed, and this one needs a human decision, so I am leaving it open. `invokeOnTimer` increments `timeouts_` **only** when `!progress_`; otherwise it clears `progress_` and counts nothing. Because a duplicate-only batch from any peer already in `requestedPeers_` sets `progress_`, that set is never cleared, and duplicate replies are free, an asked peer can hold `timeouts_` still at no cost, so `onTimer`'s failure path is never reached.

Two qualifications in fairness. It is bounded rather than indefinite: `newRound()` erases the entry, so the exposure is one keep-window, not forever. And the widened predicate was a deliberate choice, made to stop a peer that loses a fan-out race from looking like a stall. Your finding argues against that choice rather than against an oversight, which is why it needs the maintainer rather than me.

reviewCommentsList.author: bthomee
reviewCommentsList.body:
The mechanism you describe is right: `TimeoutCounter::invokeOnTimer` advances `timeouts_` only when `!progress_`, `requestedPeers_` is never erased, and a duplicate-only batch costs its sender nothing.

It is bounded rather than reverted, on `bthomee/shamap-invalid-17-duplicate-progress` (#8149), which owns the predicate. A duplicate-only batch from a peer we asked now spends from a budget of `kMaxDuplicateCredits` consecutive intervals with no useful node in between. Any batch that advances the set sets the budget back to full, and `stillNeed()` resets it when a round revives the acquisition. A credit is spent only when nothing else has answered in that interval, so a wide fan-out costs one credit rather than one per loser.

`kMaxDuplicateCredits` is `kNormTimeouts`, which is generous for the case the credit exists for: a peer that loses a fan-out race is settled in one or two intervals.

Reverting to `san.isUseful()` alone would be stricter than the base rather than equal to it. On `develop` the success path of `takeNodes` returns `SHAMapAddNode::useful()` unconditionally, so a duplicate-only batch from any sender, asked or not, sets `progress_` there.

A new case, `testDuplicateCreditRunsOut`, feeds one more duplicate-only batch than the budget holds and asserts that the last one records no progress. Removing the bound turns that case red, with one failure at the bound assertion. None of the seven existing cases that touch this predicate changed its expectation, and the suite ran green at the same count as before the change.

_The change is on the local branch and appears here on the next push of this stack._

🟠 **Severity: HIGH**

The outer batch is added to `byFee_`/`byAccount_` inside `applyImpl()` (which releases the mutex on return), then inner txs are added via `processInnerBatch()` under separate lock acquisitions. If `accept()` runs between, it can process and erase the outer batch before inner txs are added, leaving orphaned inner txs permanently blocking account sequence slots in `byAccount_`.
Helpful? Add 👍 / 👎

<details>
<summary>💡 Fix Suggestion</summary>

**Suggestion:** The race condition occurs because `applyImpl()` acquires the mutex internally at line 1767 and releases it when it returns, leaving a window between the outer batch being added and `processInnerBatch()` adding inner transactions. During this window, `accept()` can erase the outer batch, leaving orphaned inner transactions.

To fix this, ensure atomicity between adding the outer batch and all its inner transactions. Possible approaches:

1. **Restructure to hold the lock across both operations**: Refactor `applyImpl()` to optionally return without releasing the mutex (e.g., via a unique_lock that can be moved out) and pass that lock to `processInnerBatch()`, which would use it instead of acquiring its own lock for each inner tx.

2. **Move inner batch processing inside the lock**: Call `processInnerBatch()` from within `applyImpl()` after `addTxToQueue()` (around line 1880) while still holding the mutex. This requires `processInnerBatch()` to be refactored so inner `applyImpl()` calls don't try to re-acquire the mutex (use a recursive mutex, or split the locked/unlocked portions).

3. **Use a 'pending' state flag**: Add a flag to the batch's queue entry that marks it as 'pending inner txs'. Modify `accept()` to skip entries with this flag. Clear the flag after `processInnerBatch()` completes (under the lock).

Option 2 is likely the cleanest: change `txq_.mutex_` to `std::recursive_mutex`, acquire it in `apply()` before calling `applyImpl()`, and hold it through `processInnerBatch()`. All internal `std::scoped_lock` calls would be no-ops due to recursion.

</details>

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: These inners are queued as independent candidates, and `accept` later applies them one at a time without consulting the outer batch flags. That loses `tfAllOrNothing`, `tfOnlyOne`, and `tfUntilFailure` semantics: for example, a later inner can apply after an earlier inner fails, or multiple inners can apply for `tfOnlyOne`. Batch execution must remain mode-aware/atomic when dequeued.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: This cached `PreflightResult` is built with a standalone `PreflightContext`, so it has no `parentBatchId` and does not carry `TapBatch`. When the queued inner is later preclaimed, `checkSign` treats it as an ordinary transaction and the unsigned inner can be rejected; a rules/flags refresh also re-preflights it as standalone. Preserve the parent batch ID and batch apply flags in the cached result and in the queued entry.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: The Batch branch computes whether the outer entry is first in its account, but then ignores `isFirst` and checks only the inner accounts. If an inner account becomes eligible while a foreign transaction still precedes the outer Batch, `eraseAndAdvance` can schedule that blocked Batch, consuming retries and potentially dropping it.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: `isFirstInAccount` is only consulted from `eraseAndAdvance`, so the first candidate visited by `accept` is still checked only against the outer account at lines 2087-2099. A high-fee Batch whose outer account is unblocked can therefore be moved to the open ledger while an inner account is still preceded by a foreign queued transaction; when the closed-ledger Batch processing reaches that inner, `tfAllOrNothing` can discard the inners after the outer has already been applied. Apply the Batch-wide readiness check before accepting the initial candidate as well (while preserving the existing ticket ordering rules).

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: On a successful queued Batch, `MaybeTx::apply` only calls `doApply`; `Batch::doApply` returns `tesSUCCESS` without executing its inner transactions (the normal inner loop is in `applyTransaction`). Removing all inner entries here therefore discards them before any queue pass can run them, so a queued Batch advances only the outer sequence and loses the inner effects. Keep/process the inner entries as part of the Batch application instead of deleting them on outer success.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: Queue-full admission can evict an unrelated `byFee_` entry before `processInnerBatch()` has admitted all inners. If a later inner fails, this cleanup removes only the new batch and its inners; it does not restore the evicted transaction (or an evicted batch's inners). A `temINVALID_INNER_BATCH` result can therefore permanently discard unrelated queued work. Admission/eviction needs transactional rollback or all inner constraints must be checked before any eviction.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: This returns every result from `tryClearAccountQueueUpThruTx`, but that helper deliberately returns `{telINSUF_FEE_P, false}` when it cannot clear the prefix (including when it encounters a Batch inner) so the caller can fall back to normal queue admission. Returning it here rejects the candidate instead of reaching `canBeHeld()` and `addTxToQueue()`; the new Trigger 022 scenario will therefore return `telINSUF_FEE_P` rather than queueing. Only return when the result is applied.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: Batch inners are deliberately not inserted into `byFee_`, but they still run `processQueueIsFull()` here. After the outer fills `byFee_` to `maxSize_`, the first fee-free inner has level 0 and cannot beat the positive end-account average, so it returns `telCAN_NOT_QUEUE_FULL` and the whole batch is rolled back. The inner path needs to bypass the global `byFee_` capacity check while retaining per-account admission checks.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: The no-replacement rule is enforced only in `retrieveTxToReplace()`, but a high-fee Batch takes the `tryDirectApply()` path before that check. If its outer sequence/ticket matches a queued regular transaction, the Batch is applied directly and `removeFromByFee()` then erases the queued transaction, so the Batch has replaced it despite the stated restriction (the same applies to a queued Batch outer). Check for an occupied queue slot before direct-applying a Batch, or route that case through the non-replacement admission logic.

The outer's `txn` is not the same pointer as `candidate.txn` (the candidate is the outer, while the loop is checking an inner), and the outer has no `parentTx`, so this condition returns `false` and permanently holds every batch with a same-account inner. Treat the outer entry itself as belonging to the candidate batch as well as entries whose `parentTx` points to it.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: This direct-apply fast path runs before the new batch-wide `isSeqReady` check. A high-fee Batch whose outer account is ready can therefore be applied immediately while an inner's account still has an earlier queued sequence transaction. When the Batch is later processed, that inner can return `terPRE_SEQ` and be discarded by `tfAllOrNothing`, even though the outer was already accepted, which defeats the readiness/hold behavior implemented for queued Batches. Apply the same cross-account readiness check before direct-applying a Batch, or force a Batch with blocked inners through normal queue admission.

## High Level Overview of Change

Mask `secret`, `seed`, `seed_hex`, and `passphrase` fields when HTTP batch RPC requests are rejected before handler execution. Masking traverses nested objects and arrays so sensitive values are not echoed in error responses or debug reply logs.

Closes #7461.

## Context of Change

The normal RPC handler-error path masks sensitive fields before attaching request data to an error response. Eight early-error paths in HTTP batch processing instead copied the request item directly into the response, bypassing that masking.

This change applies masking only to the copied request data used by those error paths. It leaves the original request available to subsequent processing and does not sanitize successful handler output, which can legitimately contain generated wallet credentials.

## API Impact

This is a non-breaking public API bug fix. The affected error responses preserve their existing structure, codes, messages, IDs, and non-sensitive request fields; only sensitive field values are replaced with `<masked>`. `API-CHANGELOG.md` documents the change.

## Before / After

Before, an early failure such as an invalid `api_version`, forbidden method, overload, malformed method, malformed `ripplerpc`, or non-object batch item could echo sensitive request values verbatim.

After, sensitive fields in the echoed request copy are masked recursively. Other batch items continue to execute normally unless the client is already over the resource limit.

## Test Plan

- Verified the regression tests fail against the original handler with the sensitive sentinels present.
- Built the standard `xrpld` target in the repository's Nix CI environment with GCC 15.2.
- Ran all automatic RPC and server suites: 51 suites, 341 cases, 78,050 assertions, zero failures.
- Ran explicit `clang-tidy` on the changed C++ files.
- Ran applicable pre-commit checks, including the pinned formatter, include-style checks, spelling, and Markdown formatting.

issues.title: HTTP batch error paths echo full request without secret masking
issues.author: mvadari
issues.body:
1. BUG-G002: HTTP batch error paths echo full request without secret masking

*Severity*: MEDIUM *Attack vector*: AV-004

Multiple error paths in HTTP batch request processing copy the full individual request JSON into the error response without applying any sensitive-field masking. This affects: invalid API version (line 643), server overloaded (lines 685-688), forbidden (lines 700-701), null method (lines 714-715), method not string (lines 729-730), and empty method (lines 744-745). All of these either set r\[jss::request\]=jsonRPC or r=jsonRPC (copying the entire request object) without masking.

*Root cause*: The batch error handling uses shortcut error returns that bypass the masking code at lines 888-900, which only applies to the main handler execution error path for non-batch requests.

\`src/xrpld/rpc/detail/ServerHandler.cpp:643-644\`\`\`\`cppr\[jss::request\] = jsonRPC; // invalid API version, no masking\`\`\`

\`src/xrpld/rpc/detail/ServerHandler.cpp:685-688\`\`\`\`cppJson::Value r = jsonRPC; // server overloaded, copies FULL requestr\[jss::error\] = make\_json\_error(server\_overloaded, "Server is overloaded");\`\`\`

\`src/xrpld/rpc/detail/ServerHandler.cpp:700-701\`\`\`\`cppJson::Value r = jsonRPC; // forbidden, copies FULL requestr\[jss::error\] = make\_json\_error(forbidden, "Forbidden");\`\`\`

*Exploit scenario*: 1. Send HTTP batch request: \{"method":"batch","params":\[\{"method":"sign","params":\[\{"secret":"sMySecretKey"\}\],"api\_version":"invalid"\}\]\}2. The batch item fails API version validation.3. Response includes r\[jss::request\] = jsonRPC, echoing the full batch item including the nested secret in cleartext.4. Same vulnerability exists when the server is overloaded (503) or the role is forbidden (403) for batch items.

*Financial impact*: Same as BUG-G001 - secrets in batch requests that fail early validation are echoed back in cleartext.

*Invariant gap*: No masking on batch error paths. The masking logic at lines 888-900 only covers the non-batch main error path.

*Suggested fix*: Apply the same maskSensitiveFields helper on all batch error paths before including request data in responses.
